title: Mitsui & Co. and Mitsubishi Electric Benchmark Approximate and Logical QFT on Quantinuum Helios - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Mitsui & Co. and Mitsubishi Electric published joint benchmarks running the Quantum Fourier Transform on Quantinuum's 98-qubit Helios trapped-ion machine, showing physical-qubit approximate QFT degrading from P_target 0.976 at 18 qubits to 0.143 at 98, and Steane-encoded logical QFT reaching 12 logical qubits on 84 physical qubits with error detection beating active correction on fidelity but collapsing shot acceptance to 8%. Critically, non-fault-tolerant direct analog rotations still out-performed fault-tolerant code-switching T-gates at current noise levels — a candid signal that full fault tolerance is not yet economically justified.

insights.claim: Japanese industrial conglomerates Mitsui & Co. and Mitsubishi Electric co-authored and published experimental benchmarks of the Quantum Fourier Transform on Quantinuum's 98-qubit Helios trapped-ion computer, showing that large non-quantum-native corporates are now running and publishing their own hardware evaluations rather than relying on vendor claims.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Corporate end-users publishing independent benchmarks is how a technology market matures; expect vendor marketing claims to face harder scrutiny from here.
insights.quote: Experimental Evaluation of the Quantum Fourier Transform on a Trapped-Ion Quantum Computer
insights.locator: Japanese industrial conglomerates Mitsui & Co. and Mitsubishi Electric

insights.claim: The joint research team built custom quantum error correction software using Quantinuum's Guppy hybrid programming language alongside pytket compilation toolchains, evidence that Quantinuum's software stack is being adopted by external industrial R&D teams for non-trivial error-correction work.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Toolchain lock-in is the stickiest asset in quantum; external teams writing production QEC code in Guppy/pytket strengthens Quantinuum's platform moat.
insights.locator: The joint research team developed custom quantum error correction software

insights.claim: Running approximate QFT circuits across the full 98 physical qubits of Quantinuum's Helios, with the small-angle phase rotation truncation parameter set to degs=5 and leakage-detection post-selection applied, preserved a non-zero target-state probability of P_target = 0.143 at 98 qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A hard, third-party-measured fidelity number at full machine width is the kind of ground truth to benchmark competing 100-qubit-class claims against.
insights.quote: preserved a non-zero target-state probability (Ptarget​=0.143 at 98 qubits)
insights.locator: Physical Qubit Approximate QFT (Up to 98 Qubits)

insights.claim: Target-state probability for the approximate QFT fell from 0.976 at 18 physical qubits to 0.143 at 98 physical qubits, quantifying how steeply useful signal decays as circuit width scales on today's best trapped-ion hardware.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: The 0.976-to-0.143 decay curve is the practical ceiling argument against near-term physical-qubit quantum advantage; use it to discount aggressive vendor roadmaps.

insights.claim: The benchmark relied on truncating small-angle phase rotations (degs=5) to make QFT executable at 98 qubits, showing that algorithmic approximation, not just hardware improvement, is what keeps large circuits viable on current machines.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Value in near-term quantum accrues to algorithm/compiler teams that can trade exactness for depth, not only to qubit-count leaders.
insights.locator: By setting the small-angle phase rotation truncation parameter

insights.claim: Using the 7-qubit Steane error-correcting code ([[7,1,3]]), the team instantiated up to 12 logical qubits across 84 physical qubits — a 7:1 physical-to-logical overhead that consumed almost the entire 98-qubit machine to produce 12 logical qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Quantifies the brutal encoding tax on useful quantum: machines need roughly an order of magnitude more physical qubits than headline logical capability.
insights.quote: the team instantiated up to 12 logical qubits across 84 physical qubits
insights.locator: Logical QFT with Steane Code (Up to 12 Logical Qubits)

insights.claim: Error detection outperformed active error correction on logical fidelity — logical target-state probability of 0.934 at 4 logical qubits and 0.774 at 8 logical qubits — but at the cost of shot acceptance rates collapsing to 31% at 8 logical qubits and just 8% at 12 logical qubits.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: An 8% acceptance rate means ~12x runtime inflation; post-selection overhead, not fidelity, is what will price early logical-qubit compute.
insights.quote: 31% at 8 logical qubits, 8% at 12 logical qubits
insights.locator: Evaluating error-detection post-selection against active error correction

insights.claim: In a two-logical-qubit QFT test, non-fault-tolerant direct analog rotations produced higher output fidelity than fault-tolerant code-switching state injection using 30 physical qubits across quantum Reed-Muller and Steane blocks, meaning full fault-tolerant T-gate construction currently costs more than it delivers at present physical noise levels.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A rare hard data point that fault tolerance is not yet net-positive; it argues the useful-quantum timeline hinges on raw gate-noise reduction before FT architectures pay off.
insights.quote: Direct analog rotation yielded higher output fidelity under current physical noise levels, highlighting the operational overheads associated with full fault-tolerant gate construction.

insights.claim: The study frames quantum system design as a cross-layer trade-off between physical gate noise, code distance overhead and post-selection acceptance rates — a three-way constraint that any credible claim of quantum utility must satisfy simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A usable checklist for interrogating vendor logical-qubit announcements: ask for acceptance rate and code distance, not just logical qubit count.
insights.quote: cross-layer design trade-offs between physical gate noise, code distance overhead, and post-selection acceptance rates
insights.locator: The joint research team developed custom quantum error correction software
